stages.title: Opportunity cost, PPF and advantage
stages.sub: Why countries specialise and trade, built up from opportunity cost through the PPF to comparative advantage.

steps.q: A farmer has one field. Planting it with wheat means it cannot also be planted with potatoes this year. What must the farmer do?
steps.wrong: Wait until the field is bigger
steps.hint: One field, two crops that both need it. What is left to decide?

steps.q: The farmer plants wheat. Does she still get the potato harvest she did not plant?
steps.hint: Can the same field grow both crops at once?

steps.q: Could that same field instead grow potatoes, or barley, or be left as pasture?
steps.wrong: No, only wheat can be grown there
steps.hint: Is the field capable of producing just one thing, or several different things?

steps.q: Of wheat, potatoes and pasture, which one does the farmer actually count as her loss from choosing wheat?
steps.right: The single best one she gave up
steps.wrong: All the other options added together
steps.hint: She can only have picked one of the others instead. Which one would that have been?

steps.q: So what is the true cost to the farmer of growing wheat instead of potatoes?
steps.right: The potatoes she gave up producing
steps.wrong: The money she spent on wheat seed
steps.hint: Cost here is not about cash spent, it's about what was sacrificed.

steps.q: A country has a fixed amount of land, workers and machines, and can use them to make either cars or wheat. If it wants to see, for every possible split of resources, the most of each it could produce, what two things must it show on a graph?
steps.right: The maximum output of cars against the maximum output of wheat
steps.wrong: The price of cars against the price of wheat
steps.hint: Think about what is being produced with the resources, not what it sells for.

steps.q: Using all its resources, a country plots its maximum possible combinations of cars and wheat as a curve. What does that curve show?
steps.right: The maximum combinations it can produce with current resources
steps.wrong: The combinations consumers most want to buy
steps.hint: This is about production limits, not consumer preferences.
